SK2080 The set or dictionary initializer repeats a key

Two entries of one set or dictionary initializer — or of one collection expression — carry the same constant key, so the collection ends up smaller than it was written or the construction throws.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
ReSharperDuplicateKeyCollectionInitialization (resharper_duplicate_key_collection_initialization_highlighting)

Why

The three initializer forms fail in three different ways and none of them is what the author wrote. { { k, v }, { k, w } } calls Add twice and Dictionary<K, V>.Add throws ArgumentException at construction — a field initializer doing that takes the type's constructor with it. { [k] = v, [k] = w } assigns through the indexer, so the second write silently wins and v is evaluated and thrown away. new HashSet<T> { a, a } returns a set of one where two were written. In every case the object at the end of the initializer is not the object on the page, and the key is right there to compare.

Example

Instead of:

static readonly Dictionary<string, int> Weights = new() {
    ["alpha"] = 1,
    ["beta"] = 2,
    ["alpha"] = 3
};

Write:

static readonly Dictionary<string, int> Weights = new() {
    ["alpha"] = 1,
    ["beta"] = 2,
    ["gamma"] = 3
};

When it does not fire

⚠ Constant keys only. { [a] = 1, [b] = 2 } with two variables is not a finding even when a and b hold the same value at run time, because the analyzer has no way to know that and the shape is legitimate for a table built from names. An entry whose key is not a constant is skipped rather than blocking the entries around it. ⚠ The comparer is not resolved — the rule declines whenever the constructor is given any argument at all. Key equality belongs to the collection's comparer, not to the key type: new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) { ["a"] = 1, ["A"] = 2 } throws where "a" != "A" ordinally, and a comparer can just as easily make two keys the rule thinks are equal distinct. Declining on any argument is deliberately broader than declining on a comparer argument: it costs a capacity-only initializer a true finding, and it means the rule never has to decide which parameter a comparer arrived through. ⚠ The receiver must be one of `Dictionary`, `SortedDictionary`, `SortedList`, `ConcurrentDictionary`, `HashSet` or `SortedSet` as the semantic model resolves it. A List<T> may repeat an element on purpose and a user collection's Add means whatever its author wrote, so neither is examined. ⚠ The key type must be one whose default equality the analyzer can decide: string (ordinal, which is what EqualityComparer<string>.Default does), bool, char, the integral types and any enum. double, float, decimal, a nullable key and every reference type other than string are declined. Two equal constants are still equal under a sorted collection's default IComparer<T>, which is why the sorted types are in the table; the reverse — two ordinally distinct strings a culture comparer would call equal — is not reported. Only the second and any later occurrence is reported, so three copies of one key give two findings and each points at a line that can be deleted. No fix: deleting the duplicate entry and correcting its key are the two available repairs, they produce different programs, and the analyzer has no way to tell which one was meant — and deleting the entry would discard a value expression that may have side effects. ⚠ A collection expression is a different node kind, and a rule registered only on the initializer would quietly say nothing about it. new HashSet<T> { "a", "a" } and HashSet<T> s = ["a", "a"] are one defect in two spellings and the second is the idiom now, so both are examined; a spread anywhere in a collection expression withdraws the whole finding rather than being stepped over, because a duplicate the spread supplies is not this rule's to report and one it hides is not this rule's to claim. ⚠ `CA2244` overlaps the indexer form and only the indexer form, and it is not in the default .NET analysis set — measured, not assumed: an ordinary net10.0 SDK project with nothing configured reports CA2200 on a control shape and says nothing about any of these three, so a repository that has not raised AnalysisMode sees no duplicate. CA2244 also says nothing at all about the Add form, which is the one that throws at construction, or about a set that silently drops an element.
